citeAs: Amanpreet Singh, Vivek Natarajan, Meet Shah, Yu Jiang, Xinlei Chen, Dhruv Batra, Devi Parikh, Marcus Rohrbach (2019). Towards VQA Models That Can Read. CVPR 2019.
creator: Amanpreet Singh, Vivek Natarajan, Meet Shah, Yu Jiang, Xinlei Chen, Dhruv Batra, Devi Parikh, Marcus Rohrbach (Facebook AI Research, Georgia Institute of Technology)
description: TextVQA is a Visual Question Answering dataset containing 45,336 questions on 28,408 images that require reading and reasoning about text in the image to answer. Images are sourced from Open Images v3 from categories that tend to contain text (e.g., billboard, traffic sign, whiteboard), and each question-image pair has 10 ground truth answers provided by human annotators.
name: TextVQA
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: All 10 annotators agree on the most common answer for 22.8% of questions; 3 or more annotators agree on the most common answer for 97.9% of questions. Human accuracy on the dataset is 85.01% on validation and 86.79% on test, consistent with human accuracy on VQA 2.0 and VizWiz.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Three-stage crowdsourcing pipeline: Stage 1 — annotators flagged images without text using a forced-choice yes/no flag; Stage 2 — annotators provided questions requiring reading text in the image (instructed: 'Please ensure that answering the question requires reading of the text in the image. It is OK if the answer cannot be directly copied from the text but needs to be inferred or paraphrased.'); a second question with a different answer was also collected per image; Stage 3 — 10 answers were collected per question. Answer annotators were given four quality flags: (i) no text in image; (ii) not a question; (iii) answering doesn't require reading text; (iv) unanswerable. Questions where a majority of workers marked any flag were removed. Hand-crafted questions with known answers were used to identify and filter bad annotators.
rai:dataBiases: The dataset was intentionally collected from images containing text (from Open Images categories like billboard, traffic sign, whiteboard), which introduces a selection bias toward text-heavy images. The paper notes that question-only and image-only baselines achieve only 8.09% and 6.29% accuracy respectively, suggesting the dataset does not have significant biases with respect to images and questions alone. The most common answer ('yes') is the majority answer for only 4.71% of the dataset, and yes/no questions make up only 5.55%, reducing answer-distribution bias compared to VQA 2.0.
rai:dataCollection: Images were sourced from Open Images v3 dataset, selecting categories that tend to contain text (e.g., billboard, traffic sign, whiteboard). A three-stage crowdsourcing pipeline was used: (1) annotators identified and filtered images without text; (2) annotators provided 1-2 questions per image requiring reading the text to answer; (3) 10 answers were collected per question. Filtering resulted in 28,408 images forming the basis of the dataset.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Images from Open Images v3 dataset, specifically from categories that tend to contain text such as billboard, traffic sign, and whiteboard. 100 random images were sampled from each category (or all images if fewer than 100 existed), and the Rosetta OCR system was run to compute average OCR boxes per category to weight sampling.
rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Secondary Data analysis, Web Scraping
rai:dataLimitations: 8.9% of TextVQA questions can only be answered by combining multiple OCR tokens, which is not handled by the proposed model. The OCR system fails at detecting text that is rotated, unstructured (e.g., a scribble), or partially occluded. The dataset was collected from sighted humans (not visually impaired users), which may differ from real-world use cases. The diversity of answers (49.2% unique majority answers) makes it difficult to use a fixed answer space.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Images without text were filtered out via crowdsourcing (Stage 1), resulting in 28,408 images from an initial pool. Questions where a majority of workers marked quality flags (no text, not a question, answer doesn't require reading, unanswerable) were removed. Bad annotators were identified and filtered using hand-crafted questions with known correct answers. The dataset was split into train (34,602), validation (5,000), and test (5,734) sets with no image overlap between sets.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is motivated by the needs of visually impaired users, for whom reading text in images is a dominant category of questions asked of assistive devices (up to 21% of questions in the VizWiz study). Progress on TextVQA is expected to improve assistive technology for visually impaired individuals by enabling VQA models to read and reason about text in everyday images.
rai:dataUseCases: Benchmarking VQA models that can read and reason about text in images; developing assistive technology for visually impaired users (up to 21% of questions from visually impaired users involve reading text in images); encouraging research on text detection and recognition in unconstrained environments; studying the ability of VQA models to reason over unstructured external knowledge (text found in images).
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Rosetta OCR system was used to compute average number of OCR boxes per image category in Open Images, which was used to weight sampling of images for the dataset. Rosetta OCR was also used to analyze OCR token statistics reported in the paper.
